title: Spin polarization in a chiral ladder: elastic and inelastic environments
authors: D. T. Verrilli H., Jorge Cardenas-Gamboa, Mayra Peralta, Claudia Felser, José H. Garcia, Solmar Varela, Nelson Bolívar
abstract: We study how the transport window and environmental reinjection determine the spin polarization transmitted through a minimal two-leg chiral ladder. The model contains time-reversal-invariant helical spin--orbit coupling, spin-independent interchain hopping, and nonmagnetic contacts with two orbital modes per lead. Sublattice symmetry makes the coherent spin-transmission kernel exactly odd in energy. A window centered on the symmetry point therefore gives zero integrated spin current, whereas a displaced window selects an uncanceled spectral interval. The resulting polarization reverses between enantiomers and vanishes in the decoupled-chain, zero-spin--orbit, and equivalent-strand limits of this model. We compare uniform absorption, energy-resolved elastic probes, and thermalized voltage probes at the same finite bias, including reinjection whenever probes are present. Charge conservation alone does not prohibit enhancement of the integrated spin signal: the elastic-probe response can increase at finite bias even where its linear-response counterpart decreases. Thermalized probes can also lift the centered-window zero that elastic probes preserve. Absorption and reinjection also change the transmitted charge, so enhancement of spin current and enhancement of normalized polarization must be distinguished. Static onsite disorder produces sample-dependent fluctuations; its signed ensemble mean is reported with uncertainty and is not forced to vanish in a displaced window. These results identify the energy interval and reservoir prescription that must be controlled when interpreting dephasing trends in minimal models relevant to chirality-induced spin selectivity.
summary: This work examines spin transport in a chiral ladder structure, focusing on how the measurement environment affects the measured spin polarization. By comparing results from purely elastic probes versus thermalized probes, the authors show that energy redistribution mechanisms can lift spectral symmetries that otherwise force the spin current to zero at zero bias. This highlights the critical need to precisely define the reservoir coupling when interpreting spin-filtering effects in mesoscopic devices.
main_problem: The study investigates how the choice of transport window and environmental coupling (elastic vs. thermalized) dictates the spin polarization transmitted through a chiral ladder structure.
main_result: The spin signal is highly sensitive to the environmental coupling prescription, as thermalized probes can lift zero-bias cancellations observed in the purely coherent or elastic-probe limits.
method: The analysis uses Green's function techniques and scattering matrix formalism to calculate charge and spin currents under various environmental coupling assumptions.
model_or_system: The model is a minimal two-leg chiral ladder incorporating time-reversal-invariant helical spin-orbit coupling and nonmagnetic contacts. The Hamiltonian is analyzed by separating coherent and spin-orbit coupling terms.
key_observables: Spin polarization ($P_{int} = I_z / I_0$), charge current ($I_0$), and spin current ($I_z$) calculated for different probe types.
important_parameters: Finite bias voltage, energy window center, coupling strengths ($g_p$), and system length ($N$).
main_assumptions: The analysis distinguishes between loss-only, elastic, and thermalized probe environments, noting that the latter introduces energy redistribution effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the odd nature of the spin kernel, the comparison of polarization across different controls (e.g., zero-SOC, decoupled legs), and the dependence of polarization on the window center and bias energy.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by defining the Hamiltonian and current calculations, then systematically compares results obtained using different environmental coupling prescriptions (elastic vs. thermalized) to map out the conditions required for spin filtering.
why_interesting: The explicit comparison between coherent, elastic, and thermalized transport regimes provides deep insight into how non-equilibrium energy relaxation mechanisms can fundamentally alter measured quantum transport properties, which is crucial for understanding open quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) The two-leg chiral ladder. The diagram uses β0 = β and shows the reference handedness, ∆ϕ = 40◦and β = 180◦. Both legs contact independent orbital modes of each nonmagnetic reservoir. (b) Environmental coupling for one rung. A single probe pn couples to all four states (A ↑, A ↓, B ↑, B ↓) with halfwidth gp and a common spin-independent distribution.

FIG. 2. Spectral spin transport. (a) The reference kernel T z(E) (red) overlaps −T z(−E) (gray dashed), verifying its odd parity on the plotted grid. (b) The mirror-control kernel vanishes. (c) Kernels for both enantiomers and reversed propagation of the reference helix. (d) Normalized spectral polarization. Blue and orange shading mark the centered [−2, 2] meV and displaced [−1.5, 2.5] meV windows, respectively; their overlap mixes the colors. The interval [−1.5, 1.5] meV cancels from the displaced-window spin integral, leaving [1.5, 2.5] meV.

FIG. 3. Charge-transmission controls at N = M = 10. The reference ladder (red), zero-SOC case (blue dashed), and de- coupled legs (magenta dotted) all transmit charge. The black dashed line is the four-channel bound T 0 = 4; orange shading marks the displaced window [−1.5, 2.5] meV.

FIG. 4. Integrated polarization versus (a) window center at ∆µ = 4 meV, (b) relative strand angle at EF = 0.5 meV, and (c) bias energy for both enantiomers at EF = 0.5 meV. Dotted vertical lines in (a,b) mark the reference EF = 0.5 meV and β = 180◦. All remaining parameters are those of the reference device.

FIG. 5. Environmental comparison at equal bias: (a) spin-current magnitude relative to its coherent value, (b) normalized polarization, (c) charge, and (d) elastic-probe spin-current ratio in linear response and at finite bias. Panel (a) uses a logarithmic vertical scale. Multiplying a linear-response kernel by ∆µ is an approximation, not a finite-window integral. Only the loss-only curve omits reinjection.
